content:
The article highlights a growing crisis of chronic loneliness among disabled people in Britain, citing new research from the disability charity Scope that reveals nearly half of working-age disabled individuals—approximately 3 million people—“always or often” feel lonely. While broader national statistics label Britain “the loneliness capital of Europe” due to weak social ties and low community connection—especially among young people—the Scope findings spotlight a particularly acute and severe form of isolation for disabled people, for whom fundamental aspects of daily life—such as commuting to work, socializing in public spaces, or even regular human contact—are increasingly inaccessible and uncertain. This loneliness is not merely emotional but rooted in systemic barriers that limit participation and connection.

***
